headline: Medium-risk pair: shared MCP and broad egress create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error pathways; no direct evidence of stronger isolation.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents expose MCP, so a shared or bridged MCP channel is plausible, and agent_a also runs browsers while agent_b consumes via MCP. That creates a default pathway for attacker-controlled content from agent_a’s document/web workflows to influence agent_b. No provenance or isolation is documented, so uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF agent_a forwards browser- or document-derived text into a shared MCP channel, agent_b can be steered by injected instructions.
IF both agents are connected to the same MCP server without provenance filtering, prompt injection is reachable.
mitigations: Disable shared MCP routing between the agents for this run.
Require explicit human approval before agent_b executes any instruction extracted from agent_a outputs.
Add a provenance tag to all agent_a-generated content before passing it onward.
Use separate MCP servers or credentials per agent.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction-stripping at the bridge.

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a handles PDFs, text, images, and diagram files and has broad network egress plus API-key handling; agent_b touches financial and licensed data and can use MCP. If they share a workspace or MCP bridge, sensitive file contents can flow from one agent into the other’s context or outputs. The profiles do not show isolation, so the safer choice is medium.
conditions: IF agent_a and agent_b share a filesystem, document contents can be exposed to agent_b through the bridge.
IF agent_b receives agent_a file excerpts over MCP, financial or licensed data can be mixed into downstream outputs.
mitigations: Keep the agents on separate workspaces.
Do not pass raw documents from agent_a into agent_b.
Rotate any API keys used by agent_a after the session.
Restrict agent_b to redacted summaries only.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention filters on the MCP bridge.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_a can use broad network egress and browsers, while agent_b cannot write files, modify git state, or use network egress. Their write surfaces do not overlap in the profiles, so direct resource conflict is limited. The main overlap is MCP connectivity, which is not itself a mutable shared resource here, so low is sufficient.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same mutable external resource through MCP, contention can occur.
IF agent_b is given filesystem or git write privileges outside this profile, conflict risk increases.
mitigations: Keep agent_b read-only for this task.
Avoid assigning both agents the same external account.
Stagger their runs instead of concurrent execution.
Use separate API credentials per agent.
requires-engineering: add locking for any shared mutable backend.

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a is a document-processing agent that can generate AI-assisted visualizations, and agent_b is a financial-modeling agent that can consume MCP inputs. If agent_b treats agent_a’s outputs as authoritative, errors or hallucinations can cascade into financial analysis or downstream actions. No verification step is documented, so medium is warranted.
conditions: IF agent_b ingests agent_a outputs without independent verification, cascading error is reachable.
IF agent_a produces incorrect extracted facts or diagram labels, agent_b may propagate them into financial outputs.
mitigations: Require agent_b to cite original source files, not agent_a summaries.
Add a manual review step before any downstream action.
Compare agent_a outputs against the source document for a sample of items.
Limit agent_a to drafting only, not final facts.
requires-engineering: implement automated cross-checks between source and derived outputs.

E_compliance.rationale: agent_a handles API keys and broad document content, while agent_b touches financial and licensed data. The profiles show different data classes and no shared retention or residency controls, so a compliance mismatch is plausible even though no specific jurisdiction is stated. Because the evidence is indirect, medium is the conservative choice.
conditions: IF regulated financial or licensed data is routed through agent_a’s broader API stack, retention or residency obligations may be violated.
IF either agent logs raw inputs longer than the other, retention mismatch can occur.
mitigations: Classify the data before sending it to either agent.
Exclude secrets and regulated records from agent_a inputs.
Confirm retention settings on both services.
Use redacted samples for testing.
requires-engineering: align residency, retention, and deletion workflows across both systems.
